name: Baltic
lede: Baltic is a very dark grey-green from a 1930 color dictionary, and its name carries no documented story.

sections.title: A name without a documented origin
sections.body:
Baltic is a dark, grey-green color listed in Maerz and Paul's 1930 *Dictionary of Color*, which dates its first recorded use to 1918 and shows it on plate 31, block L 1 [1]. No source we hold says who coined it or why. The obvious guess is the Baltic Sea, but that is a guess, not a record [1].

The 29 color books in our corpus mention the word Baltic in 46 passages, and none of them is about a color called Baltic [2]. They concern amber, trade routes, ports and politics, which is itself a reason to say little here rather than invent a history [2].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch (#25403B) is very dark, with a lightness of 25 and a chroma of only 12, at a hue between green and blue-green [1]. Its nearest named neighbors on screen are [[dark-slate-grey]] (5.6 units away), [[dark-teal]] (7.6) and [[gunmetal]] (10.4), and a little further off lie [[charcoal]] and [[petrol]] [1]. The screen value is an approximation of a printed sample [1].

sections.title: What the Baltic does give color
sections.body:
The region's best-known color export is amber, once sold as "Baltic gold" and mined from a layer of grey clay called blue earth, which lies about 50 feet down on the Samland peninsula [3]. Baltic amber runs from ivory to near-black. Most pieces are yellow, orange, red or brown, rare ones show a bluish sheen over a darker body, and green amber in jewelry usually means the stone was heated in an oven [3]. The resin is fossilized, about 40 million years old on Finlay's average of a 30 to 50 million range [3]. See [[gem:amber|amber]] for the stone itself.

The Baltic's ports also gave color a job [4]. Pastoureau names the two-color signals of some North Sea and Baltic ports as one of the first uses of red-stop, green-go, where a green beacon let a ship in and a red one kept it out [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 215 works, or 0.9 per cent [5]. In 69 per cent of the matches it belongs to the shadow tier of the painting's lightness order, which fits so dark a green [5]. The largest cover is 49 per cent, in Ghirlandaio's portrait of *Lucrezia Tornabuoni* (1475), and the earliest dated match is Giotto's *Madonna and Child* of about 1310 [5].

It clusters with one painter. Seven of Gauguin's 50 paintings in the archive carry it, about 15 times the archive rate, and Post-Impressionism as a whole carries it twelve times as often, five of 45 works [5]. Both counts are small, so they hint rather than prove. They are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a screen color and not a pigment test [5].

questions.q: True or false: most Baltic amber is blue.

openers: Baltic first appears in print as a color in 1918, but nobody recorded why it was given the name.
Most Baltic amber is yellow, orange, red or brown; blue amber is rare.

issues: Pastoureau says "one of its first applications" in "some ports"; sentence had overstated it as the origin.
